Mortify
MOR-tih-fy
v.
From Latin mortificare, “to put to death,” from mors (death) + facere (to make). Renders the Greek nekroō, “to make dead, kill,” and thanatoō, “to put to death.”

Biblical Definition

To mortify is to put to death—specifically, to put to death the deeds of the body, the members which are upon the earth, the indwelling motions of sin which yet remain in the believer. It is the violent, deliberate, daily work of the regenerate soul against its own corruptions, in the strength of the Holy Spirit, on the ground of union with Christ. Paul’s twin texts are decisive: if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live, and mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry. The figure is not metaphor for management; it is execution. The remaining sin in the believer is not to be befriended, negotiated with, managed, or contained: it is to be killed. The Puritan John Owen’s axiom states the doctrine: be killing sin or it will be killing you. Mortification is not the work of an hour or a season but of the whole Christian life—the daily, painful, often bloody application of the cross of Christ to specific sins by the power of the Spirit. It is impossible apart from union with the crucified Christ, who broke the dominion of sin at the cross, and apart from the Spirit, by whom alone the deeds of the body are put to death. It is grievous to the flesh, because the flesh is what is being killed; it is necessary to life, because the alternative is being killed by what one refuses to kill. The doctrine of mortification rebukes both the antinomian who treats remaining sin as harmless and the moralist who tries to mortify in his own strength—and recalls the saint to the Spirit-empowered, cross-grounded, daily war on the corruptions of his own heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MORTIFY as to destroy the vital functions of; to subdue or bring into subjection by abstinence or rigorous severities; in theology, to subdue inordinate passions and appetites.

expand to see more

MORTIFY, v.t. — 1. To destroy the vital functions of; as, to mortify flesh or animal substances. 2. To subdue or bring into subjection by abstinence or rigorous severities; as, to mortify the flesh. 3. To humble; to depress; to abase, as pride; to affect with humiliating chagrin.

In theology: To subdue or destroy the activity of carnal appetites and inclinations; to bring the flesh and its lusts into subjection by self-denial and the help of divine grace.

Key Scripture

Romans 8:13 — "For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live."

Colossians 3:5 — "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry."

Galatians 5:24 — "And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts."

Romans 6:11 — "Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Modern Corruption

Mortification is corrupted, on one side, by the antinomian grace-talk that treats remaining sin as harmless and recoils from the very language of killing; and on the other, by the moralism that tries to mortify in fleshly strength rather than by the Spirit and on the ground of union with Christ.

expand to see more

Mortification is a doctrine the present church largely refuses to preach. The very word survives chiefly in the trivialized sense of I was mortified—reduced from the Spirit’s violent execution of indwelling sin to an emotion of social embarrassment. The substantive doctrine has been displaced by a soft grace-talk that treats remaining sin as either too tender to confront, too complex to address directly, or insufficiently serious to warrant violent language. The result is congregations who hear constantly that they are loved and accepted in Christ—both gloriously true—and who never hear that they are also commanded to put to death the indwelling motions of fornication, anger, covetousness, and pride that still war in their members. Antinomian grace without mortification breeds sleek, comfortable, slowly-dying souls who never learn that the gospel which justifies them also commands the daily killing of the sin from which they were justified.

The opposite corruption is moralism—the attempt to mortify in fleshly strength, by sheer willpower, by behavioral programs, by accountability software, by the discipline of the natural man. This too misses the doctrine. Biblical mortification is through the Spirit and on the ground of union with the crucified Christ: the flesh has been crucified with him, and the same Spirit who raised Christ from the dead now applies that crucifixion to the indwelling sin of the believer. Mortify in your own strength and you exchange one set of sins for another, often more religious and more dangerous. Mortify by the Spirit on the ground of the cross, and the deeds of the body are truly put to death and the soul truly lives. Owen’s great work on mortification is not optional reading for the serious saint; it is the manual of the regenerate man’s daily war against himself.

Hebrew Roots

Greek nekroō (to make dead, kill—Col 3:5) and thanatoō (to put to death—Rom 8:13), both grounded in the believer’s union with the crucified Christ.

expand to see more

Greek nekroō (G3499) — to make dead, to deaden; the verb of Col 3:5, “mortify therefore your members.”

Greek thanatoō (G2289) — to put to death; the verb of Rom 8:13, “mortify the deeds of the body.”

Greek stauroō (G4717) — to crucify; in Gal 5:24, “they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh.”

Latin mortificare — to make dead, the source of the English verb; the Vulgate’s rendering of the Greek death-verbs.

Usage

"Be killing sin or it will be killing you—Owen’s axiom states the whole doctrine in one line."

"Mortification is not metaphor for management; it is execution—the daily, Spirit-empowered putting to death of indwelling corruption."

"Antinomian grace without mortification breeds sleek, slowly-dying souls; moralism without the Spirit produces religious sins more dangerous than the ones replaced."
